subtype: Approach: reciprocity by offering something useful [Thinking]
passage:
Subject: Thinking about what I can offer

Hi Uma,

I was about to write to Dr Rao again with another "please guide me". Then I stopped, because what do I give him? He is busy, and what I want is all take. So here is my plan. He has an open-source tool for cleaning survey data, and there is a bug list. I will actually try it on my own project, note any confusing steps, and send him two clear pages. I also went to the workshop last week; I can send my notes from the sessions he missed. Hopefully it helps and starts a proper conversation. What do you think? Is that presumptuous?

Rukmini

qa.q: What will Rukmini try on the project?
qa.a: Rukmini will try the open-source tool for cleaning survey data on the project.

qa.q: What is Rukmini feeling as the email is written?
qa.a: Rukmini feels hopeful but a bit unsure, ending with a question about whether the plan is presumptuous.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rukmini use if the offer is ignored, and why?
qa.a: Rukmini could join the tool's public discussion and answer a beginner's question, because helping in public shows the same goodwill without needing a private reply.

qa.q: How might Dr Rao see this offer?
qa.a: Dr Rao would receive two clear pages about his own tool from a real user, which gives something useful instead of another request for guidance.

grounding: Shows building a relationship on what one can give, such as testing a tool or sharing notes, instead of only asking.

Hafsa, you asked how I got to know the woman who maintains that open-source mapping tool. It's Tenzin here, still a bit amazed it worked.
I'd been using her tool for my geography project for months. Everyone was messaging her with questions and requests. I thought, what does she actually need? Not another fan. Her project page said: 'Looking for testers on low-end phones.' And I have the oldest phone in our hostel.
So I spent a weekend testing it on my phone. I wrote down where the map froze and where the buttons were too small, with screenshots. Then I sent her one message: 'I tested version three on a very slow phone. Here are six problems I found. Hope it helps.'
She fixed two within a week and thanked me by name in the update notes. Later, when I asked about her career, she wrote back a whole page.

qa.q: How many problems did Tenzin report?
What was Tenzin wondering before writing to the maintainer, and how does Tenzin feel about it now?
qa.a: Tenzin wondered what she really needed instead of adding one more request, and now feels amazed and proud that offering help first worked.

qa.q: What else could Tenzin offer people in the field in future?
qa.a: A short write-up of how the tool was used in the geography project, which could help other users and show real work.

qa.q: How might the maintainer see Tenzin's message among all the requests?
qa.a: It stands out as help instead of a demand and gives her useful bug reports, which is why she fixed two and later replied warmly.

grounding: Shows a student asking what an open-source maintainer needs, testing the tool on an old phone and building the relationship around that help.

subtype: Approach: reciprocity by offering something useful [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Disha, Sudha's classmate, and I watched her do something I wouldn't have thought of. We both went to a one-day energy conference in Chennai. At lunch she pointed at a speaker, Dr Iyer, and said, 'Everyone will send him a thank-you. What would actually help him?'
She had heard him say he'd miss the afternoon panel because of a flight. So during that panel she took careful notes, and that night she wrote a one-page summary of the three main arguments and the audience questions. I saw her cut it twice to keep it short.
She emailed it to him the next morning, with one line: 'You mentioned missing this panel, so I thought this might be useful.' He wrote back the same day, thanked her, and asked about her own project. They've exchanged messages every few weeks since. I can't know what she felt, but she read his first reply aloud to me twice.

qa.q: Why did Dr Iyer miss the afternoon panel?
What might Sudha have been feeling when she read the reply aloud twice?
qa.a: She was probably excited and proud that her useful summary had opened a real conversation.

qa.q: What else could Sudha offer Dr Iyer as the contact grows?
qa.a: Share a short note on a related paper or event now and then, keeping the relationship about give and take rather than only asking.

qa.q: How does the summary look from Dr Iyer's side?
qa.a: For Dr Iyer it fills a real gap, the missed panel, so a student's email becomes something useful rather than one more thank-you.

grounding: Shows a student thinking about what a speaker needs, writing him a summary of a missed panel, and building a relationship around that help.
